statement: In New York City in 1993 to 1995, days on which that day's or the previous day's highest temperature reached 31.1 °C (88 °F) (146 of 1,095 days, here called hot days), compared with other days, were associated with more deaths certified by the city's medical examiner as unintentional cocaine overdose: 2.34 a day against 1.76 (341 deaths on hot days, 1,667 on other days), a third more (Marzuk et al., 1998); by the editors' calculation a rate ratio of 1.33 (95% CI 1.18 to 1.49), or about 85 deaths more than the other-day rate predicts, some 4 in 100 of the 2,008 cocaine overdose deaths of those three years. The days were compared without any adjustment for season, day of the week, holidays or trend, and nobody's heat exposure, amount used or pattern of use was known. Deaths from opiates without cocaine were 0.81 against 0.71 a day and other overdose deaths 0.08 on both kinds of day, neither difference significant, but by the editors' calculation the opiate rate ratio (1.14, 0.93 to 1.38) did not differ significantly from the cocaine one (ratio of the two 1.17, 0.93 to 1.47), so the paper's reading that the rise was specific to cocaine is not established; the share of homicide and traffic victims with cocaine in their blood was much the same on hot and other days (18.9 against 19.5 in 100; 9.5 against 10.3 in 100), which the authors read as cocaine use not rising on hot days; and opiates were also found in about 6 in 10 of the deaths counted as cocaine overdoses. The temperature threshold was chosen from the 1990 to 1992 overdose deaths and the dates of heat deaths with cocaine, then tested on the 1993 to 1995 deaths; of 40 tested deaths certified as due to overheating (hyperthermia) in 1990 to 1995, 10 had a breakdown product of cocaine in the body. In a laboratory experiment (Crandall et al., 2002), 7 healthy adults aged 23 to 37 who had never used cocaine were heated at rest in a suit carrying water at 46 °C after one intranasal dose of cocaine (2 mg per kg, described by the authors as low; study conditions) and, on another day in random order, after the same dose of lidocaine, a local anaesthetic used as the comparison (called placebo in the abstract): before heating, core temperature did not differ (36.79 against 36.75 °C), but during heating it rose more after cocaine (P < 0.001; to about 37.8 against 37.5 °C after about 38 minutes, read from the paper's figure and approximate); the skin's blood vessels began to widen, and sweating began, at a core temperature about 0.3 °C higher (37.37 against 37.06 °C and 37.38 against 37.07 °C; by the editors' calculation, 95% CIs of about 0.11 to 0.51 and 0.16 to 0.46 °C); at a core temperature of 37.86 °C, skin blood flow was 49 against 70 in 100 of its maximum and sweat rate 0.8 against 1.0 mg per cm² per minute (how many people reached that temperature is not stated); and people felt less hot at the same core temperature. Heat production was not measured, so the authors' conclusion that cocaine raises body temperature mainly by impairing heat loss is an inference; they expect larger doses to add heat production, say the results may not apply to people who use cocaine regularly, and did not test their suggestion that hot weather and crowded clubs amplify the effect. Neither study followed people who used cocaine in hot weather. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In New York City in the 1990s, hot days had about a third more deaths recorded as cocaine overdoses than other days (2.34 against 1.76 a day). The days were compared without allowing for season or anything else that comes with summer, and the study could not show that the rise happened only with cocaine. In a laboratory, 7 healthy people who had never used cocaine were heated after one small dose: their skin began to flush and sweat only at a higher body temperature, their body temperature rose more than after a comparison drug, and they felt less hot. Neither study looked at people using cocaine in hot weather.
population: Deaths certified by the New York City medical examiner in 1993 to 1995 (2,008 unintentional cocaine overdose deaths; 793 opiate and 85 other overdose deaths as comparisons; threshold chosen on 1990 to 1992 deaths); 7 healthy adults aged 23 to 37 who had never used cocaine, in a laboratory in Dallas

comparator: Other days; in the laboratory, the same people after the same dose of lidocaine, an active local anaesthetic control
outcome: Daily number of deaths certified as unintentional cocaine overdose (opiate and other overdose deaths, and cocaine in the blood of homicide and traffic victims, as comparisons); core temperature, skin blood flow, sweating and how hot people felt during heating

risk_of_bias.note: Day comparison (card sc_marzuk_1998): ROBINS-E high, entirely unadjusted (season, day of week, holidays and trend not modelled); deaths counted through the medical examiner's certification; the negative-control comparisons are imprecise and were not compared with the cocaine estimate. Laboratory study (card sc_crandall_2002): RoB 2 some concerns (how the order was randomized not reported; blinding not checked although cocaine raised heart rate and blood pressure, which matters for the felt heat; number contributing at the highest temperatures unknown; no protocol; about 22 comparisons without correction).

inconsistency.note: The two studies answer different parts of the question (deaths on hot days; heat-loss responses in the laboratory), and no replication of either was read.

indirectness.note: One city in 1993 to 1995 and counts of deaths per day, not anyone's own heat exposure or use; the laboratory study gave one low intranasal dose to 7 people who had never used cocaine, heated passively at rest, unlike use outside the laboratory (larger or repeated amounts, exertion, other drugs).

imprecision.note: Seven people in the laboratory, with the intervals for the comparisons at 37.86 °C close to no difference; the opiate comparison cannot exclude a rise of about a third. The cocaine rate ratio itself is precise (1.18 to 1.49).

large_effect.note: Not applied: a rate ratio of 1.33 from an unadjusted comparison.

dose_response.note: Not applied: the paper's 'steady increase' above the threshold rests on cumulative and moving-average curves without a test of trend (card reporting issues).

grade.reasoning: The day comparison is observational and starts low; rated down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, it is very low. The laboratory study, rated alone, would start high as a randomized crossover and be rated down for risk of bias, indirectness (one low dose in people who had never used cocaine, at rest) and imprecision (7 people), also very low. 'Is associated with': the death counts come from an unadjusted comparison of days, and the laboratory study shows what one dose did to heat-loss responses under passive heating, not what happens to people who use cocaine in hot weather. Status single study: each part rests on one study; the laboratory study is consistent with the death counts but does not replicate them, and it takes them as its starting point. Not read: the editorial on the New York study (Kilbourne, 1998), the published letter on the laboratory study with the authors' reply (Schier et al., 2002), a later study of the same association (Auger et al., 2017) and population studies of heat and drug deaths on the reading list. The post-mortem cocaine levels that the laboratory paper's introduction cites are second-hand and not used.

statement: Among 116 adults in Australia who had used ecstasy at least once, surveyed in 2004 through the researchers' acquaintances and their networks and through an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter (Allott & Redman, 2006; 51 in 100 women, mean age 26.5), every respondent reported at least one thing they did to avoid ecstasy's negative side effects, chosen from a list: most often drinking water (96 in 100), limiting the amount of ecstasy (71 in 100), taking breaks or chilling out (62 in 100), a healthy lifestyle (60 in 100) and vitamins or natural products (53 in 100); 30 in 100 took other illegal drugs and 16 in 100 prescription medicines for this. To avoid the comedown in the days after, 4 in 100 had no strategy, and to avoid brain damage, 18 in 100 had none. 41 in 100 had taken pharmaceuticals or natural products before ecstasy ('preloading') and 47 in 100 after it ('postloading'): among those who listed them, half took multivitamins and 41 in 100 took 5-HTP (a building block of serotonin) before, followed by magnesium and fruit or juice, and 46 in 100 took 5-HTP and 44 in 100 multivitamins after; among those who gave reasons, 46 in 100 did it to ease the comedown and 33 in 100 to reduce brain damage. About 39 in 100 had ever tested their pills (61 in 100 never had; editors' calculation), and 53 in 100 had changed how they used ecstasy because of something they disliked about it, most of them by using it less often. Every respondent had also used at least one other substance with ecstasy, most often alcohol (91 in 100 before and 81 in 100 during use) and amphetamines (60 in 100 before and 66 in 100 during). Preloading and postloading were more common among respondents who had used ecstasy more than 50 times (preloading 55 against 30 in 100), among about 30 tests without correction. These figures describe one self-selected sample, not how common the practices are: respondents found through harm-reduction websites may be more interested in harm reduction, the response rate is unknown, the questionnaire was not validated, and how often each strategy was used was not asked. Whether any of these practices lowers harm was not studied: the authors note that the evidence that preloading protects comes only from studies in rodents given injected pre-treatments, and that taking 5-HTP, SSRI antidepressants or St John's wort with ecstasy may risk serotonin syndrome, which this survey did not examine. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a 2004 survey of 116 people in Australia who had used ecstasy, almost all said they drank water to avoid side effects, and most said they limited how much they took or took breaks. About 4 in 10 had taken vitamins, 5-HTP or other products before ecstasy, and about half afterwards, mostly to ease the comedown; about 4 in 10 had ever tested their pills. Many were found through harm-reduction websites, so this is not how common these habits are. Whether any of them lowers harm was not studied, and the authors warn that 5-HTP and some antidepressants taken with ecstasy may risk serotonin syndrome.

statement: In adults with panic disorder diagnosed by a clinician and tested in laboratories while off psychiatric medicines, a single oral dose of caffeine of 400 to about 750 mg (480 mg in 7 of 10 studies; study conditions), compared with a placebo of the same or similar taste in the same people, increases the chance of a panic attack within hours, by a meta-analysis of 10 small blinded challenge studies published from 1985 to 2015 (Klevebrant & Frick, 2022): in the 9 studies that reported panic attacks, 121 of 237 people with panic disorder (51 in 100) had one after caffeine, and no study reported one after placebo; in the 6 studies that also tested people without panic disorder, 69 of 128 people with panic disorder (54 in 100) had one after caffeine against 2 of 115 healthy controls (2 in 100), a difference of 52 in 100 (editors' calculation). The paper prints two incompatible pooled risk ratios for that comparison (about 32 by its text and 12.1 in its figure), so the counts are the better summary. Self-rated anxiety rose after caffeine in both groups, more on average in people with panic disorder (standardized difference 1.02, 95% CI 0.09 to 1.96), but the studies varied widely (prediction interval −1.27 to 3.32; about 0.72 without one outlying study, editors' recalculation), and these rises were measured after caffeine without a placebo comparison, which only 2 studies reported. The authors equate 480 mg with about 5 cups of brewed coffee at about 100 mg a cup, so the doses tested correspond to about 4 to 7.5 such cups taken at once (editors' calculation); no study tested less than 400 mg, so what everyday amounts do in panic disorder is not known. All studies were done at rest during a break from psychiatric medicines; 2 always gave caffeine last, and 8 of the 10 come from two research groups. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In small laboratory studies, about half of adults with panic disorder had a panic attack after one large dose of caffeine (121 of 237), and none after a dummy drink or capsule. Among people without panic disorder, 2 of 115 had one. The doses were like 4 or more cups of coffee at once, and smaller amounts were never tested, so what a cup or two does is not known.
population: Adults with panic disorder diagnosed by a clinician (DSM-III to DSM-5 or ICD criteria), mostly recruited from outpatient clinics and tested during a break from psychiatric medicines: 244 people in 10 studies (1985 to 2015), and 122 psychiatrically healthy controls in 7 of the studies
exposure: A single oral dose of caffeine given blind at rest: 480 mg in 7 studies, 400 mg in 1, and 10 or 7 mg per kg in 2 (about 750 and 525 mg at 75 kg), as capsules, instant coffee or other drinks (study conditions)
comparator: Placebo with the same or similar taste in the same people (all studies); healthy controls given the same challenge (7 studies)
outcome: Panic attack within 30 to 240 minutes (self- or clinician-reported); change in self-rated anxiety
magnitude: Klevebrant & Frick (2022): panic attacks after caffeine 121/237 (51.1%) with panic disorder in 9 studies and 2/115 (1.7%) controls; none after placebo in any study. In the 6 studies with both groups 69/128 (53.9%) against 2/115 (1.7%), risk difference 52.2 percentage points (editors' calculation); pooled log RR 3.47 (95% CI 2.06 to 4.87) in the text, which is RR about 32 (7.8 to 130; editors' calculation), against RR 12.12 (6.06 to 24.23) in Fig. 4. Studies without controls: 52/109 (47.7%). Anxiety change after caffeine (6 studies; 121 with panic disorder, 111 controls): g 1.94 (1.19 to 2.69) and 0.91 (0.46 to 1.36); difference g 1.02 (0.09 to 1.96), I² 66.8%, prediction interval −1.27 to 3.32; about 0.72 (0.07 to 1.37) without the outlying study (editors' recalculation). Doses 400 to about 750 mg, about 4 to 7.5 cups of brewed coffee at about 100 mg a cup (editors' calculation from the authors' equivalence of 480 mg with about 5 cups).

The review itself is AMSTAR 2 critically low (card sc_klevebrant_2022): two incompatible pooled risk ratios, an inconsistently described model, risk of bias never discussed, English-language published reports only.

inconsistency.note: All six studies with both groups point the same way, and about half of the people with panic disorder had an attack in the studies with and without controls (54 and 48 in 100); the anxiety results vary more but are described, not graded.

indirectness.note: Single doses of 400 to about 750 mg taken at once, at rest in a laboratory, during a break from psychiatric medicines; everyday intake, people on treatment and life outside the laboratory were not studied.

imprecision.note: The proportions rest on 237 people with panic disorder and 115 controls and agree across studies; the unstable pooled ratio is not used.

publication_bias.note: No small-study effect was seen for panic attacks; with six studies no test is possible, and the search excluded unpublished and non-English reports. Not rated down.

grade.reasoning: Blinded placebo-controlled within-person challenge studies start high; rated down for risk of bias (two fixed-order studies, assessor blinding mostly unclear, and a review whose pooled ratios disagree) and indirectness (single large doses at rest in a laboratory, off medication): low. 'Increases' rests on the within-person comparison with placebo: about half had a panic attack after caffeine and none after placebo. The comparison with healthy controls is not randomized and is shown as counts, not as a ratio. The anxiety results are described, not graded: they are changes after caffeine without a placebo comparison, with a prediction interval that includes no difference. The primary studies were not read; the counts are the review's text and Table 1. Status replicated: 9 studies from at least two independent research groups point the same way, though studies within each group are not independent of each other.
